source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: Lockheed Palo Alto built the first fielded CBR system, for autoclave loading (the CLAVIER lineage). Expert knowledge sat in a few heads and there was no theory.
numbers: Development began 1987. In regular use since fall 1990. Low-risk development strategy.
quote: the first fielded CBR system was developed
limits: Review text gives no throughput or savings figure for Lockheed. Primary sources (Mark 1989; Hennessy and Hinkle 1992) were not opened.
agent_relevance: Deployed CBR started where experts hold unwritten precedent. Our agent's case store fits the same niche: no clean rule set, many past episodes.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: General Dynamics Electric Boat moved from rules to CBR for valve selection after rule brittleness and maintenance problems.
numbers: Rule system started 1986. CBR feasibility 1988. Fielded 1990. By fall 1991 used in 3 of 4 departments. 20,000 non-conformances handled Dec 1990 to Sep 1991.
limits: Cost figures are the review's own summary of a company report (Brown 1991). Not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Rules were brittle and costly to maintain, cases were less so. Same argument as for scaffolds versus hard-coded procedures.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: Only quantified economic claim in the review: CBR cut about 10 percent of previous manual handling cost.
numbers: CBR and rule system each cost 5 man-years; 750,000 USD total. About 10 percent cost reduction, 240,000 USD saved in under a year.
limits: Baseline is the manual procedure, not the rule system. No control group. Single site.
agent_relevance: Deployment evidence of that era was payback figures, not controlled accuracy tests.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: The rule base was reused to structure cases and seed the first case base before fielding.
numbers: Seed from existing rule base, fielded 1990.
limits: Anecdotal, single system.
agent_relevance: Seeding a case store from an existing procedure is a cheap cold start for our agent.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: Help desk systems were the fastest growing deployed CBR type. Retrieved cases were shown as information chunks to the user, not used for reasoning.
numbers: Described as rapidly growing by 1994. No counts given.
limits: Review claim, no adoption statistics.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-only use (no adaptation) was the common deployed form. This matches RAG-style use of cases in LLMs.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: Commercial CBR shells appeared in 1991 and were reviewed by 1992. They traded flexibility for speed of building.
numbers: Shells: ReMind, CBR Express/ART-IM, Esteem, Induce-it/CasePower, KATE-CBR, ReCall, S3-Case. ReMind offered inductive, nearest-neighbour and SQL-like retrieval.
limits: Feature description only. No head-to-head tests.
agent_relevance: Deployed CBR leaned on simple retrieval (nearest neighbour, decision-tree index). Heavy adaptation was rare.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: Stated motives for CBR: incremental learning from every solved problem, and decision support that lets non-experts and new staff do expert work.
numbers: Lockheed aims: let non-experts do the job and help train new staff.
limits: Stated as motives. No measured training effect in the review.
agent_relevance: Retain step is the core benefit claim. Our schema should test it, not assume it.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches
finding: By 1994 the review said CBR could not yet boast many fielded applications, and detailed only two.
numbers: Two detailed fielded systems.
limits: Small sample. Published deployment stories are success-biased.
agent_relevance: Treat deployment stories as weak evidence.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento casts an LLM agent as case-based reasoning: store (state, action, reward) cases, retrieve, plan with a GPT-4.1 planner and o3 or o4-mini executor.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3, top-1. GAIA test 79.40%. DeepResearcher avg 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. SimpleQA 95.0 PM. HLE 24.4 PM.
limits: Leaderboard result with a heavy planner and tool stack, not an isolated CBR test. Test score uses a case bank built on validation.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence that a case bank works in a deployed-style agent, but see the ablation lines for how much is CBR.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Ablation separates CBR from planning and tools. CBR adds a smaller, consistent gain on top of planning.
numbers: CBR gain over Memento without CBR (F1/PM): HLE +4.5/+7.0, SimpleQA +3.7/+5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7/+8.2. Planning gain: DeepResearcher +29.1/+11.5.
quote: case-based reasoning provides consistent, additive improvements
limits: One backbone pair (gpt-4.1 + o4-mini). No seeds or confidence intervals reported.
agent_relevance: Honest size of the case-memory effect: roughly 4 to 7 F1 points, far less than planning plus tools.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Number of retrieved cases: a small memory is best. Gains saturate at K=4 and decline slightly later.
limits: Differences after K=1 are under 1 point, probably within noise. One benchmark set.
agent_relevance: Retrieve few cases (1 to 4). Most of the effect arrives with the first retrieved case.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Continual learning over five iterations: learned (parametric) case retrieval beats plain similarity retrieval, which beats no CBR, but gaps are small and shrink.
numbers: DeepResearcher PM, iter 1 to 5: no CBR 78.65, 80.93, 82.62, 83.53, 84.47. Non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85. Parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
limits: Gap between no CBR and parametric CBR falls from 1.8 points (iter 1) to 1.0 (iter 5). The planner alone also improves with repeat iterations.
agent_relevance: Part of an apparent learning curve is not due to cases. Control for repeat exposure.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Out-of-distribution test: cases from NQ, TQ, HotpotQA, 2Wiki help on held-out MuSiQue, Bamboogle, PopQA.
numbers: Absolute gains 4.7 to 9.6 points with 4 retrieved cases (Fig. 1d). Table 5 F1: Musique 35.6 to 40.6, Bamboogle 77.5 to 86.2, PopQA 57.9 to 64.0.
limits: Different datasets but similar QA style. The paper itself notes contamination on DeepResearcher sets.
agent_relevance: Case transfer across datasets is modest but positive.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: A fast planner beat a slow planner on GAIA validation (pass@1). Concise planning outperformed deliberate planning.
limits: Confounded by planner model family. Authors give trace-based reasons only.
agent_relevance: Over-long plans can mislead the executor. Keep planning steps short.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Tools can hurt without planning: the online executor lost to the offline executor on DeepResearcher.
numbers: Offline 48.8/62.8 vs online 30.8/60.7 F1/PM (-18.0 F1, -2.1 PM). Authors suspect data contamination.
limits: Contamination explanation not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: external retrieval is not automatically helpful.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal QA
finding: CBR-RAG on legal QA: retrieve full cases (question, support, answer) with hybrid embeddings, feed to Mistral-7B.
numbers: Case base 2,084 cases (2,124 minus 40). No-RAG cosine 0.8967. Best: Hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 full case 0.9141, about 1.94% above No-RAG. Support-only at k=3: 0.9092.
limits: Metric is embedding cosine to a reference answer, not human or factual accuracy. High baseline because of parametric memory.
agent_relevance: Case retrieval gain is small on a metric where the base model already scores high.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal QA
finding: Significance is weak: only the best variant clears the bar, and only with one-tailed tests.
numbers: AnglEBERT k=3 beats No-RAG and LegalBERT k=3 at 95% (one-tailed t-test). Versus hybrid BERT k=1 only at 90%.
limits: One-tailed tests, multiple comparisons, no effect sizes, no human check. Differences about 0.017 cosine.
agent_relevance: Do not overread small retrieval gains on cosine metrics.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal QA
finding: Putting the full case in the prompt beat support text alone in most variants, with exceptions.
numbers: Hybrid BERT k=1 full 0.9068 vs support 0.8986. Exception: AnglEBERT k=1 support 0.9121 vs full 0.9074.
limits: Mixed. Differences under 0.01.
agent_relevance: Case form (whole episode versus extracted fact) matters little here.

source: Zhao et al. (2023/2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: ExpeL (cases plus extracted insights, no parameter updates) beats ReAct on three agent benchmarks. Insights and case recall help different tasks.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38% SR. Full ExpeL vs ReAct: HotpotQA 39.0 vs 28.0; ALFWorld 59.0 vs 40.0.
limits: GPT-3.5/4 API models, 4-fold validation, small test sets. Few-shot prompts taken from ReAct.
agent_relevance: Case retrieval fits action-heavy tasks (ALFWorld). Abstracted rules fit reasoning tasks. Use both.

source: Zhao et al. (2023/2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Retrieval ranking matters: retrieve cases by task similarity, not by reasoning-step similarity or at random.
numbers: ALFWorld SR: ReAct 40.0, random cases 42.5, reasoning-similarity 48.5, task-similarity (ExpeL) 59.0.
limits: One environment, one variant of each retrieval type.
agent_relevance: Similarity function is a large lever. Random cases give almost nothing.

source: Zhao et al. (2023/2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Insight extraction ablation: LLM-written insights beat human-written ones. Adding reflection text hurt. A better extractor model was better.
numbers: HotpotQA SR: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted 32.0, with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL (gpt-4) 39.0.
limits: One environment, small n.
agent_relevance: Insight source quality matters. Stronger models write better case summaries.

source: Zhao et al. (2023/2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Transfer from HotpotQA to FEVER works, and combines with Reflexion retries.
numbers: FEVER SR: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer w/o task demos 65, ExpeL transfer 70. ALFWorld R3: ReAct+Reflexion 54.4, ExpeL retrieve-only 60.4, ExpeL+Reflexion 64.2.
limits: Related task pair. Reflexion rounds start from failed R0 checkpoints.
agent_relevance: Cases transfer across related tasks. Retry loops add on top.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent Workflow Memory stores reusable sub-routines instead of whole cases. It beats concrete-example retrieval.
numbers: WebArena SR 35.5% vs BrowserGym 23.5 (51.1% relative gain). Mind2Web 24.6% relative gain. Versus Synapse example retrieval: +5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step SR.
limits: Many WebArena tasks share templates, so a cross-template subset was needed to show generalisation.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a case into a workflow generalises better than raw cases.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Self-induced workflows can be wrong. Online induction (no training data) tied offline in-domain and gained as domain gap grew, but absolute Mind2Web success stayed in single digits.
numbers: Workflow action space variant: +1.3 step SR, same overall SR 3.2, workflows called in 18.5% of tasks. Rule vs LM induction on WebArena: 0.1 gap in SR.
limits: Low absolute success on Mind2Web. Numbers from text, not re-derived from tables.
agent_relevance: Self-induced cases can be wrong. Add a check before retaining.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion stores verbal lessons from failed trials. Close to case retention without cases.
numbers: ALFWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with ReAct+Reflexion over 12 trials; ReAct alone plateaus between trials 6 and 7. Reported gains over baselines: 22% ALFWorld, 20% HotPotQA, 11% HumanEval.
limits: Uses environment success signal and a hallucination heuristic. Same-task retries.
agent_relevance: Retention works when a reliable success signal exists.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: Voyager's skill library is a case base of executable programs, reused by retrieval.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x baselines. Wooden tool 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x faster.
limits: Minecraft only. Skill library confounded with curriculum and self-verification.
agent_relevance: Reusable executable precedent compounds. Our agent may keep verified snippets.

source: Majumder et al. (2023) CLIN: A Continually Learning Language Agent
finding: CLIN keeps a causal-insight memory across trials on a frozen LLM.
numbers: Beats Reflexion by 23 absolute points (ScienceWorld). Zero-shot transfer +4 points (13 for new tasks), then +17 more with memory updates (7 for new tasks).
limits: ScienceWorld only. Paper warns specific insights like 'go to desk 1' may hurt in new tasks.
agent_relevance: Store general causal lessons, not task-specific steps.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Case-Based or Rule-Based: How Do Transformers Do the Math?
finding: Boundary evidence: fine-tuned transformers do math by similar-case lookup, not rules.
numbers: Leave-Square-Out: random split 100% accuracy but held-out squares fail away from the boundary. Rule-following fine-tuning: Llama-2-7B 91.1% at 9-digit addition vs scratchpad under 40%; GPT-3.5 over 95% at 12 digits from 100 samples.
limits: GPT-2 and small fine-tuned models on five toy tasks. Not retrieval-based CBR.
agent_relevance: Case-like behaviour fails far from seen cases. Pair cases with explicit rules for systematic tasks.

source: Mark (1989) CLAVIER, Lockheed autoclave
finding: Original CLAVIER source was not opened. Known only through Aamodt and Plaza.
numbers: none
limits: Not read. No numbers taken from it.
agent_relevance: Open Mark 1989 and Hennessy and Hinkle 1992 in a later pass.

source: Cheetham (2005) GE Plastics Color Formulation Tool
finding: Not opened. Web search budget was exhausted and direct AAAI URL guesses failed.
numbers: none
limits: No claim recorded.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a long-run deployed CBR result with maintenance data.
